newsitem.title: BELGIUM: East Europe uneasy over French summit idea.
newsitem.headline: East Europe uneasy over French summit idea.

text.p: Former communist states in central and eastern Europe clamouring to slip under NATO's protective shield expressed deep misgivings on Thursday over French ideas of a "big power" summit to meet Russian concerns.
"This is an unfortunate idea," Poland's Foreign Ministry spokesman Pawel Dobrowolski told Reuters. "It is an initiative which could be applauded by opponents of our accession plans."

Several of Russia's former Warsaw Pact allies said the proposal for a meeting of France, Russia, Germany, the United States and Britain was uncomfortably close to a "Yalta-style" approach to the continent's security questions.
"This is a throw-back to the 19th century way of doing things, not what you would expect as we move into the 21st," said one eastern European source.

In 1945, the Stalinist Soviet Union and Western states signed the Yalta agreement which effectively divided the continent into east and west and prevented central European states from joining the European-Atlantic institutions.

But despite evident unease over the idea , which flies in the face of U.S. assurances of a "step-by-step, open and democratic" way of dealing with enlargement, the leading candidates hinted they could live with it if it ended Moscow's opposition.
"If it further complicates the enlargement issue then it
is quite simply a disaster, but if this is the only way to a solution then so be it," said an ambassador from central Europe.
Hungary reacted cautiously to the French proposal.
"It is in our interest that the process of enlargement goes unhindered," Hungary's Foreign Ministry spokesman Gabor Szentivanyi told Reuters.
"We welcome it if a dialogue between NATO and Russia addresses the concerns that have come up but as to what form this dialogue would take is entirely up to NATO," he added.

Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are leading the field to win admission to NATO first time around, with Romania and Slovenia close behind. The new applicants are set to be named at a special summit in Madrid in July.
Russia has been offered a special charter with NATO to run in parallel with alliance enlargement, but so far has shown no sign of dropping its virulent opposition to the plan.

The United States has reacted frostily to the French idea, which has predictably received the enthusiastic backing of Moscow. Analysts say they fear the Russians have spotted an opportunity to cash in on alliance differences over how to proceed.
"The Russians are looking for cracks in alliance solidarity and will exploit any they find, I fear they have found one," added the ambassador.

He and other eastern European diplomats in Brussels said they were worried the summit idea would undermine NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana's position as the alliance's front-man in talks with the Russians.

Solana, strongly backed by the United States and in close contact with the allies, has held one round of talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and is due to hold another in Brussels on February 23.

Diplomats said on Thursday that German Chancellor Helmut Kohl had backed the idea of a security summit, suggested for April -- only a few weeks before a proposed summit between Presidents Boris Yeltsin and Bill Clinton.

Analysts said on Thursday the French proposal underlined European concerns not to be presented with any "fait accompli" by the United States, which historically deals with Russia on a bilateral basis on many fronts.
